set.detail:
Septimius Odaenathus belonged to a leading family of Palmyra that had held Roman citizenship since the Severans; by the 250s he was a senator of consular rank and 'exarch' (ras) of Tadmor. Inscriptions show him already prominent before Valerian's capture. When Shapur's army withdrew from Cilicia and Syria in 260, Odaenathus attacked its rear on the Euphrates, seizing booty and part of the royal harem. In 261 he destroyed the last of the Macriani, Quietus, at Emesa, and Gallienus, unable to come east, made him his commander there, with titles later attested for him and his son as dux Romanorum and corrector (or restitutor) totius Orientis.

In 262 Odaenathus, with Palmyrene cataphracts, mounted archers and the remains of the Roman eastern army, crossed into Mesopotamia, retook Carrhae and Nisibis (whose inhabitants, according to the Historia Augusta, had sided with Persia), and advanced down the Euphrates to Ctesiphon, which he besieged without taking. A second expedition followed around 266-267, again reaching the Persian capital. He took the title King of Kings, crowning his eldest son Herodes (Hairan) as co-king, in deliberate rivalry with Shapur, while Gallienus celebrated the victories on his own coins and took the title Persicus Maximus.

Odaenathus was murdered with Herodes in 267 or 268, at Emesa or Heraclea Pontica, by a relative named Maeonius, in circumstances later blamed on Zenobia or on Gallienus. Historians debate his status: was he a loyal Roman official who saved the east for Gallienus (as Zosimus, Festus and Zonaras suggest), a client king, or an independent ruler laying the foundation of the Palmyrene empire of Zenobia? Udo Hartmann's study stresses the ambiguity of a man who was simultaneously Roman senator, governor and an Oriental 'King of Kings'. Persian sources are silent, and Shapur's later inscriptions do not mention him.

scholarship: Hartmann, Das palmyrenische Teilreich (2001)
Andrade, Zenobia: Shooting Star of Palmyra (2018)

set.detail:
In 267 or 268 a great coalition of Heruli and Goths from the Sea of Azov built a fleet, said by Syncellus to number 500 ships, sailed through the Bosporus, failed before Byzantium, where the Roman fleet won a skirmish, and broke into the Aegean. They plundered Cyzicus, Lemnos and Scyros and landed in Greece, sacking Corinth, Argos and Sparta and attacking Athens. The city's old walls had been repaired under Valerian, but the Heruli took and burned it, devastating the Agora, the Library of Pantainos and much of the lower city; destruction layers and coin hoards in the American Agora excavations are dramatic.

The Athenian historian Publius Herennius Dexippus, a former archon, rallied 2,000 Athenians in the woods outside the city and harassed the raiders. A fragment of his Scythica preserves the speech he claims to have made to them, in the style of Thucydides, and an inscription honours him. With the help of a Roman fleet under Cleodamus and Athenaeus, the Athenians forced the Heruli to withdraw. In 2014 newly deciphered palimpsest fragments of Dexippus in Vienna (the Scythica Vindobonensia) revealed further fighting at Thermopylae and in Thessaly and Boeotia. The invaders moved north, where Gallienus defeated them on the Nestus in 268 and won over the Herul chief Naulobatus.

Afterwards the Athenians built the so-called post-Herulian wall, enclosing only a small area north of the Acropolis with rubble from destroyed buildings, a vivid image of the shrinkage of classical cities. Later legend, reported by Zonaras and others, has the Goths about to burn Athens' libraries until one argued that they should leave the Greeks their books to keep them unwarlike. Date (267 or 268) and sequence remain disputed.

scholarship: Millar, "P. Herennius Dexippus: The Greek World and the Third-Century Invasions", JRS 59 (1969)
Martin et al., "Scythica Vindobonensia", Wiener Studien 127 (2014)

set.detail:
Early in 268 Aureolus, commander of Gallienus' new mobile cavalry force based at Milan and a former shepherd from the Danube, rebelled, perhaps first declaring for Postumus and then claiming the throne himself. Gallienus hurried back from the Balkans, defeated him at a bridge over the Adda later called Pons Aureoli (Pontirolo) and shut him up in Milan. During the siege a conspiracy formed among the senior officers: the praetorian prefect Aurelius Heraclianus, the general Marcianus, the commander of the Dalmatian cavalry Cecropius and, according to Aurelius Victor and Zosimus, the future emperors Claudius and Aurelian. One night Cecropius brought news that Aureolus was making a sortie; Gallienus rushed out with only a few guards and was run through by a spear or javelin. He died in late summer, probably August or September 268, after fifteen years of rule.

The army, devoted to Gallienus, mutinied and had to be calmed with a donative of 20 aurei per man. Claudius, proclaimed emperor, asked the Senate to deify Gallienus and halted a massacre of Gallienus' relatives and supporters that the Senate had begun in Rome, where his brother and surviving son were killed. Aureolus surrendered and was killed. The Historia Augusta, written in a later Constantinian climate that claimed Claudius as Constantine's ancestor, takes pains to exonerate him.

The Latin tradition, shaped by senators bitter at Gallienus' exclusion of senators from command, portrays him as a frivolous voluptuary. Modern scholars (de Blois, Geiger) emphasise instead his achievements: survival through usurpations, plague and invasion, creation of a central cavalry reserve, promotion of professional officers, toleration of Christians, and patronage of Plotinus. His murder by the 'Illyrian' officers he had promoted opened the line of soldier emperors who completed the recovery.

scholarship: de Blois, The Policy of the Emperor Gallienus (1976)
Geiger, Gallienus (2013)

set.detail:
The invasion of 268-269 was the largest Gothic incursion of the century. Zosimus' figures of 320,000 warriors and 6,000 ships, and the Historia Augusta's 2,000 ships, are absurd, but the coalition of Goths, Heruli, Peucini and others was clearly vast. After failing before Tomis and Marcianopolis and losing ships in the Bosporus, they besieged Cassandreia and Thessalonica, then moved north up the Axius when Claudius approached. Near Naissus in Moesia Superior Claudius brought them to battle. Zosimus says the Romans were at first pressed hard, but that a flanking movement by troops on an unexpected route turned the tide and 50,000 barbarians were killed.

The survivors, fortified behind their wagons, retreated into the Haemus mountains, where Roman cavalry under Aurelian harassed them; cut off from supplies in winter and ravaged by the plague, they dissolved. Many surrendered and, as the Historia Augusta says, the provinces filled with Gothic slaves and farmers, and Goths were enrolled in the army. A naval detachment that raided Crete, Rhodes and Cyprus was destroyed. Claudius took the title Gothicus Maximus, but died of the plague at Sirmium early in 270.

The victory became central to Constantinian propaganda after 310, when Constantine claimed descent from Claudius, and the Historia Augusta inflates it into a Roman Salamis. Modern debate concerns chronology and credit: some scholars (notably Bray and others) argue that the decisive battle was fought by Gallienus in 268 (identified with or following the Nestus victory) and later transferred to Claudius by the Constantinian tradition. Most accept a Claudian victory in 269. Either way, the Gothic threat on the Danube was broken for a generation, enabling Aurelian's campaigns in the east and west.
set.debate: Whether Naissus was won by Gallienus (268) or Claudius (269).

scholarship: Bray, Gallienus (1997)
Wolfram, History of the Goths (1988)

set.detail:
After Odaenathus' murder his widow Septimia Zenobia ruled in the name of their son Vaballathus, who inherited his father's titles of King of Kings and corrector of the east. In 270, after Claudius' death, Palmyra moved decisively. The general Septimius Zabdas, reportedly with 70,000 men, invaded Egypt with the help of an Egyptian collaborator, Timagenes. The prefect Tenagino Probus, returning from operations against pirates, recovered Alexandria and drove out the Palmyrene garrison, but was outmanoeuvred near Babylon (Old Cairo) by Timagenes, who knew the terrain, and killed himself. Egypt, the empire's granary, passed under Palmyrene control, while other forces occupied Arabia, destroying the temple of Jupiter Hammon at Bostra, garrisoned by legio III Cyrenaica, and pushed through Asia Minor to Ancyra, attempting Chalcedon.

Zenobia did not at first claim independence. Coins at Antioch and Alexandria in 270-272 paired Aurelian (as Augustus) on the obverse with Vaballathus as 'vir clarissimus, rex, imperator, dux Romanorum' on the reverse, and papyri date documents by both rulers. Only in 272, as Aurelian approached, did Vaballathus take the title Augustus and Zenobia that of Augusta. Her court included the philosopher Cassius Longinus, and later sources depict her as learned, chaste and ambitious, claiming descent from Cleopatra.

Historians debate her aims. Some see a bid for independent eastern empire; others (Andrade, Hartmann) see an attempt to secure for her son the eastern command and perhaps the imperial title within a Roman framework at a moment when the central regime was weak. Whatever the intention, control of Egypt and Asia Minor threatened Rome's grain supply and could not be tolerated, and Aurelian launched his eastern campaign in 272.

scholarship: Hartmann, Das palmyrenische Teilreich (2001)
Andrade, Zenobia (2018)
Southern, Empress Zenobia (2008)

set.detail:
Trajan's Dacia, the only Roman province north of the lower Danube, had been under pressure from the Carpi, Goths and other peoples since the 240s. Coin circulation and inscriptions in the province end around 256-260, and many scholars think that Roman control had already effectively collapsed under Gallienus. The formal decision came under Aurelian, probably in 271 after his Gothic victory, or perhaps in 272-275. Eutropius writes that Aurelian, despairing of keeping Dacia since Illyricum and Moesia had been devastated, withdrew the Romans from its cities and fields and settled them in the middle of Moesia, calling it Dacia, so that it now divided the two Moesias.

The new Dacia, carved from Moesia Superior and Inferior, was soon divided into Dacia Ripensis on the Danube, with its capital at Ratiaria where legio XIII Gemina was transferred and V Macedonica at Oescus, and Dacia Mediterranea inland around Serdica and Naissus. The surrendered territory came under the control of the Tervingian Goths, Taifali and Carpi, though Constantine later built a bridge across the Danube at Oescus-Sucidava (328) and held bridgeheads on the north bank.

The question of what happened to the Latin-speaking population has been politically charged since the eighteenth century. The Romanian 'continuity theory' holds that a Daco-Roman population remained and became the ancestors of the Romanians; the 'immigration theory' of Robert Roesler (1871) argues that Romance speakers moved north of the Danube in the Middle Ages. Archaeology shows some continuity of Roman-style material culture and early Christian objects, such as the fourth-century Biertan donarium with its chi-rho, but no proof either way. The withdrawal was a rational shortening of the frontier and showed Aurelian's readiness to abandon a symbolically important conquest.

scholarship: Opreanu, "The North-Danube Regions from the Roman Province of Dacia to the Emergence of the Romanian Language", in History of Romania: Compendium (2006)
Ellis, "Dacia Terra Deserta", Dacia 42 (1998)

set.detail:
The Juthungian invasion of Italy in 270-271, which defeated Aurelian at Placentia and caused panic in Rome, prompted the emperor to give the capital its first new wall since the Republic. Begun in 271, the circuit ran about 19 km, enclosing roughly 13.7 square kilometres including the Campus Martius and Trastevere. The original wall was a concrete core faced with brick, about 3.5 m thick and 6-8 m high, with a square tower every hundred Roman feet (about 29.6 m), giving 381 towers and around 18 main gates, plus posterns. To save time and money it incorporated existing structures: the Castra Praetoria, the Amphitheatrum Castrense, the Pyramid of Gaius Cestius, the arches of aqueducts at Porta Maggiore, and stretches of tombs and houses. Malalas says the citizens themselves were drafted to build it, and the guilds probably supplied labour. It was completed under Probus by about 279.

The wall was designed against raiding war bands without siege equipment, not regular armies. Maxentius raised and improved parts of it in preparation for war with Constantine, and under Honorius in 401-403, with Stilicho, it was doubled in height, with a covered gallery and rebuilt gates, the form in which the Visigoths found it in 408-410. Belisarius defended it during the Gothic siege of 537-538. It remained the city's defence until Italian troops breached it at Porta Pia on 20 September 1870, and long stretches survive.

The wall marks a symbolic turn: the capital of the empire, which had trusted to the frontier armies for 300 years, now needed physical protection, as did dozens of Gallic and Italian towns whose late Roman walls are smaller still. Hendrik Dey argues that it also reshaped the city's identity and later Christian topography.

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Dey, The Aurelian Wall and the Refashioning of Imperial Rome, AD 271-855 (2011)

set.detail:
After defeating the Palmyrene army under Zabdas at Immae near Antioch and again at Emesa in 272, Aurelian marched across about 150 km of desert to Palmyra, harassed by Bedouin raiders but supplied, Zosimus says, by the cities of Syria. Zenobia had refused his terms; the Historia Augusta gives an exchange of letters in which she cites Cleopatra's choice of death over submission, almost certainly an invention. Aurelian surrounded the oasis city, whose walls had been strengthened, and starved it while bringing in supplies by caravan from the conquered regions.

Realising that Persian help, promised or hoped for, would not arrive (Shapur I had just died or was dying), Zenobia slipped out of the city on a female camel to seek aid from Persia, but was caught by Roman horsemen as she was about to cross the Euphrates. Palmyra then surrendered, in the summer of 272. Aurelian spared the city but took its treasure and left a garrison under Sandarion. At Emesa Zenobia was tried before a tribunal; according to Zosimus she blamed her advisers, and the philosopher Cassius Longinus was executed, meeting his death calmly.

Zenobia's fate is reported differently: Zosimus says she died, by illness or hunger strike, on the way to Rome; the Historia Augusta and other Latin sources say she was led in gold chains in Aurelian's triumph of 274 and then given a villa at Tibur, where she lived as a Roman matron and married into the aristocracy. In 273 Palmyra revolted again under Septimius Antiochus and Apsaeus, killing the garrison; Aurelian returned and sacked the city, which never recovered its commercial importance, though it later became a Diocletianic legionary fortress. The campaign reunited the east and Egypt with the empire.

scholarship: Andrade, Zenobia: Shooting Star of Palmyra (2018)
Watson, Aurelian and the Third Century (1999)

set.detail:
By 270 the radiate coins that made up the bulk of the money supply contained around 2 per cent silver or less, often struck on crude, light flans; forgeries and barbarous imitations circulated widely, and in 271 the mint workers of Rome, implicated in fraud, rose under their chief Felicissimus and were suppressed with thousands of deaths. After reuniting the empire, Aurelian reorganised the coinage in 274. He closed the Rome mint temporarily, opened or reorganised others (Lugdunum, Ticinum, Siscia, Serdica, Cyzicus, Antioch, Tripolis, Alexandria), and issued a new, heavier radiate of about 3.9-4 g with a guaranteed silver content of about 5 per cent, carefully struck with a silver surface. Its reverse bears the mark XXI or, in Greek mints, KA.

The meaning of XXI is the most disputed question in late Roman numismatics. The most widely accepted explanation is a ratio of twenty parts copper to one of silver (5 per cent fineness); alternatives read it as 'twenty units (nummi or sestertii) equal one' denomination, or as a value of 20 asses or 2.5 denarii. Aurelian also struck a heavier aureus at 50 to the pound and introduced a laureate denarius and bronze fractions. Zosimus says he distributed the new silver and called in the debased coin.

The immediate effect was paradoxical. In Egypt prices recorded on papyri jumped roughly tenfold soon after 274, suggesting that the new coin was overvalued by decree or that the old coin was retariffed downward, triggering a surge of inflation that continued to Diocletian's reforms. The reform's coin types, showing Sol and the legend 'Deus et dominus natus' at Serdica, also expressed Aurelian's theology of power. Diocletian replaced the system in 294, but Aurelian's centralised mint network and marked fineness laid its foundations.
set.debate: Meaning of XXI/KA: 20:1 alloy ratio versus a tariff of value.

scholarship: Estiot, Monnaies de l'Empire romain XII.1: D'Aurélien à Florien (2004)
Harl, Coinage in the Roman Economy (1996)

set.detail:
The Gallic Empire had been weakened by the murders of Postumus (269), Marius and Victorinus (271), the secession of Spain and Narbonensis, and Germanic raids. Its last emperor, Gaius Pius Esuvius Tetricus, a senator and governor of Aquitania, proclaimed at Burdigala in 271, made his son Tetricus II Caesar and moved the court to Trier. After returning from the east, Aurelian invaded Gaul early in 274 and met the Gallic army on the Catalaunian Fields near Durocortorum and Châlons-en-Champagne.

The Latin tradition (Eutropius, Aurelius Victor, the Historia Augusta) claims that Tetricus, tired of his mutinous troops, had secretly offered to surrender, quoting Virgil to Aurelian ('Eripe me his, invicte, malis', 'snatch me from these evils, unconquered one'), and deserted his army during the battle. The Gallic soldiers fought on with great loss of life before surrendering. The story may well be propaganda that excused Tetricus, who was spared and later given an administrative post as corrector Lucaniae (or of part of Italy), where, the Historia Augusta says, Aurelian addressed him as colleague. Tetricus and his son were displayed in Aurelian's triumph in 274 alongside Zenobia.

The battle reunited Britain, Gaul and Spain with the central empire after fourteen years, and Aurelian took the title Restitutor Orbis. The bloodshed, however, weakened the Rhine defences, and in 275-276 Franks and Alamanni ravaged Gaul so badly that the Historia Augusta speaks of 60 or 70 cities taken, which Probus had to recover. Aurelius Victor also mentions a short-lived revolt of a certain Faustinus at Trier around this time. The battlefield's exact location is unknown.
set.debate: Truth of Tetricus' betrayal; exact site and date (early 274).

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

scholarship: Drinkwater, The Gallic Empire (1987)
Watson, Aurelian and the Third Century (1999)

set.detail:
Carus' Persian expedition ended in 283 with his death near Ctesiphon, by lightning according to the official story. His younger son Numerian led the army back west, travelling in a closed litter because of an eye infection. Near Nicomedia, in November 284, the soldiers noticed the smell of decay and found him dead; suspicion fell on his father-in-law, the praetorian prefect Arrius Aper, who had concealed the death. On 20 November 284 an assembly of the army outside Nicomedia chose as emperor Diocles, commander of the imperial bodyguard (protectores domestici), a Dalmatian of humble origin, possibly the son of a scribe or freedman, born around 244 near Salona.

Standing on a tribunal before the troops, Diocles swore by the sun that he had no part in Numerian's death, accused Aper and ran him through with his own sword. The Historia Augusta adds that a Druidess in Gaul had once told him he would be emperor when he had killed a boar (aper), and that he had hunted boars in vain until this moment. He took the name Gaius Aurelius Valerius Diocletianus and the consulship. Carus' elder son Carinus, ruling the west, defeated the usurper Sabinus Julianus and marched against Diocletian, winning the battle of the Margus in 285 before being killed by his own officers. Diocletian notably kept Carinus' prefect Aristobulus in office and avoided purges.

The accession marks the conventional end of the third-century crisis and the beginning of 'late antiquity' in many textbooks. Diocletian reigned for over twenty years, the longest since Antoninus Pius, and created the Tetrarchy, the enlarged provincial system, new taxation and coinage, and the last great persecution of Christians, before abdicating in 305. Modern biographies (Kolb, Leadbetter, Roberto) emphasise his pragmatism and experimentation rather than a master plan.

scholarship: Barnes, The New Empire of Diocletian and Constantine (1982)
Leadbetter, Galerius and the Will of Diocletian (2009)

set.detail:
Marcus Aurelius Valerius Maximianus, born around 250 near Sirmium to shopkeeper parents, was a veteran officer of Aurelian and Probus and an old comrade of Diocletian. After the defeat of Carinus, Diocletian, facing simultaneous threats in the east and the west, made him Caesar in July 285, probably at Milan, and sent him to Gaul against the Bagaudae, rural rebels led by Amandus and Aelianus, whom he quickly suppressed. Maximian was then raised to Augustus, probably on 1 April 286 (some scholars date the promotion later in 286 or even to 287), becoming Diocletian's colleague rather than his heir; Diocletian had no son, and Maximian's son Maxentius was a child.

By 287 the two rulers had adopted the signa Jovius and Herculius: Diocletian was protected by Jupiter, ruler of the gods, and Maximian by Hercules, his helper and son, a theology that expressed both partnership and hierarchy. Maximian ruled the west from Milan and Trier, campaigning against Alamanni, Burgundians, Heruli and Franks, while losing Britain to Carausius (286) and failing in a naval expedition against him (289). The panegyrics of 289 and 291 celebrate the harmony of the two Augusti, whose meeting at Milan in the winter of 290-291 is staged as an epiphany.

The dyarchy was the first step towards the Tetrarchy of 293. It embodied the idea that the empire was too large and too threatened for one ruler, and established the pattern of regional imperial courts that lasted until 476. Maximian remained, as Lactantius complains, the rougher partner, but was loyal to Diocletian until his reluctant abdication in 305; his later attempts to regain power (306-310) ended in his death at Massilia. The precise chronology of 285-286 depends on papyri, coins and the panegyrics and is still debated.
set.debate: Date of elevation to Augustus (1 April 286 or later).

scholarship: Kolb, Diocletian und die Erste Tetrarchie (1987)
Rees, Layers of Loyalty in Latin Panegyric AD 289-307 (2002)

set.detail:
Over the decades after 293 the roughly 50 provinces of the Severan empire were divided into about 100 smaller units. The Laterculus Veronensis, a list of provinces preserved in a seventh-century manuscript at Verona and dated to around 314, gives twelve dioceses with their provinces: Oriens, Pontica, Asiana, Thraciae, Moesiae, Pannoniae, Britanniae, Galliae, Viennensis, Italia, Hispaniae and Africa. Each diocese was supervised by a vicarius ('deputy of the praetorian prefects'), forming a new tier between the governors and the prefects. Italy lost its privileged status: it was divided into districts under correctores and subjected to the land tax, with a distinction between Italia annonaria in the north, which fed the court and army, and Italia suburbicaria, which supplied Rome. Egypt was split into several provinces (Aegyptus Iovia, Herculia, Thebais), and Asia, Syria and Africa into smaller units.

The purpose was to bring government closer to the taxpayers, to make the new tax system workable, and to reduce the power of individual governors to rebel. Gradually, and not fully until Constantine, civil governors (praesides, consulares, correctores) were separated from the military commanders (duces) of frontier districts. The number of officials rose sharply: Lactantius, hostile, complains that the provinces were chopped into fragments and that there were more people receiving salaries than paying taxes.

The chronology is uncertain. Barnes and others place most divisions under Diocletian between 293 and 305; Constantin Zuckerman and others argue that the dioceses were created only around 313-314 under Constantine and Licinius. The system lasted, with modifications, until the seventh century, and the dioceses later shaped ecclesiastical geography, since metropolitan sees and patriarchates largely followed provinces and dioceses.
set.debate: Dioceses created c. 297 (Diocletian) or c. 313-314 (Constantine and Licinius).

scholarship: Barnes, The New Empire of Diocletian and Constantine (1982)
Zuckerman, "Sur la liste de Vérone et la province de Grande Arménie", Travaux et Mémoires 14 (2002)
Jones, The Later Roman Empire 284-602 (1964)

set.detail:
On 1 March 293 the two Augusti each appointed a Caesar: Maximian chose Flavius Valerius Constantius, his praetorian prefect, at Milan, and Diocletian chose Gaius Galerius Valerius Maximianus, a former herdsman from Dacia Ripensis, probably at Sirmium (Lactantius implies Nicomedia). Both Caesars were adopted into the families of their Augusti and married to their daughters or stepdaughters: Constantius had already put aside Helena, mother of Constantine, to marry Maximian's stepdaughter Theodora, and Galerius married Diocletian's daughter Valeria. The Caesars received the signa Herculius and Jovius respectively.

The four rulers shared the empire's wars while governing it as a single college: laws and coins were issued in all four names, and statues showed them as interchangeable, as in the porphyry group now at San Marco in Venice, brought from the Philadelphion in Constantinople, with its embracing pairs. Each had a regional sphere and residences: Constantius in Trier fighting Carausius and the Franks, Maximian in Milan and Aquileia, Galerius in Sirmium and later Thessalonica, Diocletian in Nicomedia and Antioch. The panegyric of 297 compares the four rulers to the elements, seasons and other natural fours.

The term 'Tetrarchy' is modern; contemporaries spoke of Augusti and Caesars. Historians debate whether Diocletian intended a system of succession by merit and adoption, as the abdication of 305 suggests (Kolb), or improvised a structure in response to military needs (Barnes, Leadbetter). It was effective in war, winning back Britain (296), Egypt (297-298) and victory over Persia (298), but it ignored dynastic loyalty: in 306 the armies proclaimed the sons of Constantius and Maximian, and the second Tetrarchy dissolved into civil war.

scholarship: Kolb, Diocletian und die Erste Tetrarchie (1987)
Rees, Diocletian and the Tetrarchy (2004)

set.detail:
Around 294 Diocletian replaced the remnants of the third-century coinage with a uniform imperial system struck to the same standards and types in a network of mints that eventually numbered about fifteen, each marked on the coins: Londinium, Treveri, Lugdunum, Ticinum, Aquileia, Roma, Carthago, Siscia, Serdica, Thessalonica, Heraclea, Nicomedia, Cyzicus, Antiochia and Alexandria. The gold aureus was set at 60 to the pound (about 5.4 g); a new silver coin, the argenteus, of almost pure silver at 96 to the pound (about 3.4 g), revived the standard of Nero's denarius; and a large bronze coin of about 10 g with a small silver content, the nummus (called follis by modern collectors), carried the reverse GENIO POPVLI ROMANI. Smaller radiate and laureate bronze fractions completed the system.

The local civic and provincial coinages of the east, including the billon tetradrachms of Alexandria, came to an end (the last Alexandrian tetradrachms date to 296/297), so that a single Roman currency now circulated across the empire for the first time. The reform was accompanied by the tax reform and, in 301, by a currency edict known from an inscription at Aphrodisias that doubled the face value of the coins, and by the Price Edict.

The nominal values of the coins in denarii (the unit of account) are uncertain, and the reform did not stop inflation: the nummus soon shrank, falling to about 1/96 pound by 318 under Constantine and his rivals. Gold, however, became the anchor of the late Roman monetary system, especially after Constantine's solidus. Numismatists (Sutherland, Hendy, Harl) see 294 as the creation of the late Roman coinage; debates concern the tariffs of the coins and how far the state deliberately used retariffing to manage its finances.

scholarship: Sutherland, RIC VI (1967)
Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy c. 300-1450 (1985)
Harl, Coinage in the Roman Economy (1996)

set.detail:
The Roman state of the third century had come to rely on ad hoc requisitions in kind (indictiones) to feed the army as the coinage collapsed. Diocletian systematised them. An edict of Aristius Optatus, prefect of Egypt, dated 16 March 297 and preserved on a papyrus from Karanis (P.Cair.Isid. 1), announces that the emperors have fixed a just assessment so that each person may know what he owes, according to the quality of land and the number of people (capita) on it. Land was measured in units (iuga) adjusted for productivity: the Syro-Roman lawbook gives, for Syria, 5 iugera of vineyard, 20 of first-class arable, 40 of second-class or 60 of third-class land as one iugum, with olive trees counted by number. People and animals were counted as capita. A census, at first every five years and from 312 in a fifteen-year cycle, the indiction, determined each province's liability, and each year the government published the rate per unit needed to meet the budget.

The system made state revenues predictable and spread the burden more systematically, and the indiction became a standard way of dating documents into the Middle Ages. But it also tied people to the land and to their occupations: to keep the tax base fixed, laws bound coloni to estates, decurions to city councils and members of essential guilds to their trades. Lactantius describes the census-takers torturing people to make them declare more than they owned and taxing even the dead. Over the fourth century much of the tax in kind was commuted into gold (adaeratio).

Modern scholars (Jones, Carrié, Bransbourg) debate whether iugatio and capitatio were a single system or two separate taxes, and how uniform it was across the empire; Egypt, Syria, Asia and Gaul show different practices.

scholarship: Jones, The Later Roman Empire 284-602 (1964)
Carrié and Rousselle, L'Empire romain en mutation (1999)

set.detail:
In 296 Narseh, son of Shapur I and King of Kings since 293, invaded Roman Armenia and Mesopotamia. Galerius, sent against him, was defeated between Callinicum and Carrhae in 296 or 297. According to Eutropius, Festus and Ammianus, Diocletian then humiliated his Caesar by making him run a mile in front of his carriage in his purple robes, although some modern historians read the scene as a misunderstood ceremonial. Galerius raised a new army of veterans and recruits from Illyricum and Moesia, perhaps 25,000 strong, and in 298 attacked through Armenia, where the terrain favoured infantry and the population was friendly.

According to Festus and Eutropius, Galerius personally reconnoitred the Persian camp with two companions and then fell on it by surprise, perhaps at night or at dawn. Narseh, wounded, fled; his camp was taken with his treasury, his harem, his wife Arsane, his sisters and children and many nobles. The site is usually located near Satala in Armenia Minor, though the evidence for the name is weak and some prefer a location in Greater Armenia. Galerius then advanced into Media and Adiabene and probably reached Ctesiphon, though it is unclear whether he took it.

The victory was celebrated on the Arch of Galerius at Thessalonica, where Galerius is shown on horseback fighting Narseh and the Persian royal women are captured. Petrus Patricius preserves the scene in which Narseh's envoy Apharban appealed to Galerius to remember that Rome and Persia were the two eyes of the world, and Galerius angrily reminded him of the treatment of Valerian. The battle led directly to the Peace of Nisibis and was the greatest Roman victory over the Sasanians, restoring Roman prestige in the east for a generation and boosting Galerius' standing within the Tetrarchy.
set.debate: Location of the battle (Satala or elsewhere in Armenia) and whether Galerius took Ctesiphon.

scholarship: Leadbetter, Galerius and the Will of Diocletian (2009)
Dodgeon and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars (1991)

set.detail:
After his defeat in 298 Narseh sought peace to recover his family. Diocletian and Galerius met at Nisibis and sent the magister memoriae Sicorius Probus to Narseh in Media, where, according to Petrus Patricius, he was kept waiting until the Persian king had gathered his forces before being received on the river Asprudis. The terms, as preserved by Petrus, were: the cession to Rome of five regions east of the Tigris (listed by Petrus as Intelene, Sophene, Arzanene, Corduene and Zabdicene, while Ammianus, recording their loss in 363, names Arzanena, Moxoena, Zabdicena, Rehimena and Corduena); the Tigris to form the boundary; the frontier of Armenia to be at the fortress of Zintha on the border of Media; Rome to appoint the king of Iberia; and Nisibis to be the sole place of trade between the empires. Narseh accepted all the terms except the trade clause, according to Petrus, but was forced to yield. His family was returned.

The treaty, usually dated to 299 (some argue 298), marked the high point of Roman power in the east. It placed Roman garrisons beyond the Tigris, secured Armenia under Tiridates III, whose conversion to Christianity followed in the early fourth century, and brought Iberia into the Roman orbit. Diocletian strengthened the frontier with the Strata Diocletiana and new forts.

The peace held for almost forty years. Shapur II, who had come of age by the 330s, refused to accept it, and war resumed at Constantine's death in 337. The Transtigritane regions became the main prize of the long war that culminated in Jovian's surrender of them, with Nisibis, in 363. Modern scholars (Blockley, Winter) debate the exact list of regions and whether the trade clause was designed to control commerce or to channel customs revenue.

scholarship: Blockley, East Roman Foreign Policy (1992)
Winter, "On the Regulation of Trade in the Treaty of 298", in Studies in Roman Warfare (1990)

set.detail:
Issued at the end of 301 in the names of the four rulers, the Edict on Maximum Prices is known from over 40 inscriptions and fragments, mostly from the Greek-speaking eastern provinces (Aphrodisias, Stratonicea, Aezani, Corinth, Egypt and elsewhere), Latin and Greek, which together preserve most of its text. Its long preamble, in convoluted official rhetoric, blames the 'raging avarice' of profiteers who exploit soldiers on the march by charging four or eight times the fair price, so that a soldier loses his donative and pay in a single purchase. It fixed maximum prices and wages in denarii for more than a thousand items, with death as the penalty for selling above them, for hoarding, or for buying at higher prices.

The list ranges from foodstuffs and wine to textiles, leather, timber, animals and services, with sea freight rates between named ports. A military modius of wheat was set at 100 denarii; the daily wage of a farm labourer at 25 denarii with food, of a carpenter or baker at 50; a teacher of rhetoric could charge 250 denarii per pupil per month. Wines were graded: ordinary wine was capped at 8 denarii per Italian sextarius, while the finest Italian wines, Falernian and others, and Maeonian from Lydia could fetch up to 30, and Pannonian and Gallic beer 4. A pound of purple-dyed silk cost 150,000 denarii.

Lactantius, a witness in Nicomedia, says the edict caused much bloodshed over trivial goods, that goods vanished from the market, and that it was eventually abandoned. Its economic logic is still debated. Some see it as an attempt to make the new currency work after the doubling of its face value earlier in 301; others as a policy aimed mainly at army supply. For historians it is an unparalleled source for relative prices, wages and the regional economy of the late Roman world.

sources.w: Edictum de pretiis (ed. Lauffer 1971, with later Aphrodisias fragments)

scholarship: Lauffer, Diokletians Preisedikt (1971)
Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (2nd ed., 2000)

set.detail:
By 303 Christians held offices in the palace, the army and the provinces, and a large church stood in Nicomedia opposite the imperial palace. Lactantius blames Galerius and his mother Romula for urging Diocletian to persecute; Diocletian consulted his council and the oracle of Apollo at Didyma, which complained that 'the just on earth' prevented it from speaking truly. Intellectual attacks on Christianity accompanied the campaign: Sossianus Hierocles, governor of Bithynia, wrote the Philalethes comparing Christ unfavourably with Apollonius of Tyana.

On 23 February 303, the feast of the Terminalia, soldiers demolished the Nicomedia church. The first edict, published the next day, ordered churches destroyed and scriptures surrendered and burned, banned Christian assemblies, deprived Christians of high rank of their privileges and the right to appear in court, and reduced imperial freedmen to slavery. After two fires in the palace were blamed on Christians, a second edict ordered the arrest of the clergy, a third (for the vicennalia in November 303) released those who sacrificed, and a fourth, in early 304, required everyone to sacrifice. Enforcement varied: in the west Constantius, Lactantius says, only pulled down churches, while Maximian enforced the edicts in Italy and Africa; in Galerius' and Maximinus' east the persecution continued with interruptions until 311 and, under Maximinus, until 313. Eusebius describes the burning of the church at Nicomedia with its congregation, mass executions in the Thebaid and martyrdoms in Palestine.

Geoffrey de Ste Croix estimated some 3,000-3,500 executions; others suggest fewer. The crisis created the problem of the traditores who had handed over scriptures, the root of the Donatist and Melitian schisms, and a cult of martyrs that shaped Christian identity. It was the last and most severe attempt by the Roman state to suppress Christianity.

scholarship: de Ste Croix, "Aspects of the Great Persecution", HTR 47 (1954)
Frend, Martyrdom and Persecution in the Early Church (1965)

set.detail:
Diocletian fell gravely ill after his vicennalia in Rome in late 303; Lactantius says he collapsed in December 304 and was believed dead, appearing in public again in March 305 so changed as to be scarcely recognisable. According to Lactantius, Galerius pressed him to retire, threatening civil war, and to appoint Caesars of Galerius' choosing. A panegyric of 307 adds that Maximian had sworn an oath in the Capitoline temple during the vicennalia that he would abdicate with Diocletian.

On 1 May 305, on a hill three miles outside Nicomedia where Galerius had been made Caesar, with a statue of Jupiter on a column, Diocletian addressed the troops in tears, saying he was old and needed rest. The soldiers expected Constantine, who was standing on the platform, and Maxentius to be named; instead Diocletian announced Severus, a heavy-drinking officer and friend of Galerius, and Maximinus Daia, Galerius' nephew. Galerius brought Maximinus forward, removed his private dress and Diocletian put his own purple cloak on him. Diocletian then rode in a carriage through the city to his native Dalmatia and the palace he had built at Split. On the same day Maximian abdicated at Milan in favour of Severus. Constantius and Galerius became Augusti.

It was the first voluntary abdication by a reigning Roman emperor. When in 308 Galerius asked him to return to power at the conference of Carnuntum, Diocletian replied, according to the Epitome, that if they could see the cabbages he grew with his own hands at Salona, they would never ask him to exchange that happiness for power. The succession of 305, which excluded the sons of emperors, soon collapsed with the proclamations of Constantine and Maxentius in 306, and Diocletian lived to see his system destroyed and his wife and daughter murdered.

scholarship: Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (1981)
Leadbetter, Galerius and the Will of Diocletian (2009)

set.detail:
Constantine, born at Naissus on 27 February around 272-273 to Constantius and Helena, spent his youth at Diocletian's court, serving in the Persian and Danubian wars and witnessing the outbreak of the persecution at Nicomedia. Passed over in 305, he obtained permission to join his father, who was preparing an expedition against the Picts, and reached him at Gesoriacum. Father and son campaigned north of Hadrian's Wall in 305-306. Constantius died at Eboracum on 25 July 306. His army, at the instigation of the Alamannic king Crocus, who commanded auxiliaries, at once proclaimed Constantine Augustus.

The circumstances were later shaped by propaganda. Lactantius and Eusebius have the dying Constantius designating his son and the army fulfilling his will; the panegyric of 310 claims Constantine resisted the soldiers and spurred his horse to escape the purple. In reality the proclamation broke the Tetrarchic rules of 305, under which Severus should have become Augustus in the west. Galerius, receiving Constantine's laureled portrait, wanted to burn it but, to avoid war, recognised him only as Caesar and promoted Severus to Augustus; Constantine accepted the lower rank. He ruled Britain, Gaul and Spain from Trier, fought the Franks and Bructeri, built the Cologne bridge and, in 307, married Maximian's daughter Fausta and accepted the title Augustus from Maximian.

The proclamation at York was the first step in a career that ended with Constantine as sole emperor (324) and the transformation of the empire into a Christian state. A modern bronze statue outside York Minster commemorates it. Historians debate whether Constantius had deliberately planned the succession by summoning his son, as Barnes thinks, or whether the army acted on its own; either way it reasserted the dynastic principle that the Tetrarchy had sought to suppress.

scholarship: Barnes, Constantine: Dynasty, Religion and Power in the Later Roman Empire (2011)
Potter, Constantine the Emperor (2013)

set.detail:
Marcus Aurelius Valerius Maxentius, son of Maximian and the Syrian Eutropia, son-in-law of Galerius through his marriage to Valeria Maximilla, had been passed over in 305 and was living as a private citizen on an estate on the Via Labicana outside Rome. In 306 Galerius planned to extend the census and taxation to the people of the city of Rome, hitherto exempt, and to abolish the remaining Praetorian cohorts. On 28 October 306 the Praetorians, a few tribunes (Marcellianus, Marcellus) and Lucianus, who controlled the free distribution of pork, proclaimed Maxentius; the vicar of the prefect who resisted was killed. Maxentius at first styled himself princeps, not Augustus, perhaps hoping for recognition, and called his father out of retirement; Maximian resumed the purple.

Italy and Africa recognised the new regime. When Severus invaded Italy in early 307, his troops, many of them Maximian's veterans, deserted, and Severus surrendered at Ravenna and was later killed. Galerius invaded in the summer of 307 but found Rome's walls too large to besiege and withdrew, his troops plundering on the way. In 308 Maximian tried to depose his son and fled to Constantine. Africa revolted under Domitius Alexander (308-309/310), cutting Rome's grain supply and causing famine until Maxentius' prefect Volusianus crushed the revolt.

Maxentius presented himself as conservator urbis suae, the champion of Rome and its traditions, and built lavishly: the Basilica Nova, the restored Temple of Venus and Roma, a villa, circus and mausoleum on the Via Appia. He ended the persecution in his territories and restored Christian property in 311. The Constantinian tradition made him a tyrant, oppressive and debauched; modern scholarship (Cullhed) presents a more traditional Roman ruler whose regime collapsed at the Milvian Bridge in 312.

scholarship: Cullhed, Conservator Urbis Suae: Studies in the Politics and Propaganda of the Emperor Maxentius (1994)

set.detail:
Diocletian had struck the aureus at 60 to the pound. Around 309-310, at the Trier mint, Constantine began striking a lighter gold coin at 72 to the Roman pound, about 4.5 g, which came to be called the solidus ('solid' or 'whole'). The term appears in laws by 325, and the 72 solidi to the pound also fixed the late Roman reckoning of gold by weight: a solidus equalled 24 siliquae (carats, from the carob seed), the origin of the modern carat. Constantine's solidus circulated first in his western territories; after the defeat of Licinius in 324 it became standard empire-wide, and the eastern aureus at 60 to the pound disappeared.

Constantine's ability to maintain the solidus rested on large stocks of gold: Anonymous De Rebus Bellicis and Eusebius link it to the confiscation of temple treasures after 324, and taxes such as the chrysargyron (collatio lustralis) and senatorial levies were paid in gold or silver. Gold coins were used for state payments to soldiers and officials, and much taxation in kind was progressively commuted into gold. Valentinian I's reforms of 366-368 refined the metal (marked OB) and centralised its minting at the imperial court.

The solidus was the most successful coin in history in terms of stability: it kept its weight and nearly pure fineness in the Byzantine empire (as the nomisma) until debasement began in the 1030s-1040s, and it served as an international currency from Britain to India; Indian and Chinese finds attest its reach. The flip side was that bronze coinage for everyday use continued to inflate against gold. Jairus Banaji argues that the gold economy created a new aristocracy of service; others stress continuity. The date is debated (309 or 310, some say 312), but Trier is certain as the first mint.

scholarship: Banaji, Agrarian Change in Late Antiquity: Gold, Labour and Aristocratic Dominance (2001)
Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy (1985)

set.detail:
When Mensurius, bishop of Carthage, died around 311 (some date it 307), his archdeacon Caecilian was quickly consecrated by local bishops including Felix of Abthugni, who was accused of having been a traditor, one who surrendered scriptures in the persecution. Caecilian had made enemies by restricting the veneration of martyrs not officially recognised, including that of a wealthy woman, Lucilla, who was accused of kissing a dubious martyr's bone before communion. A council of some 70 Numidian bishops under Secundus of Tigisis, primate of Numidia, declared Caecilian's consecration invalid and elected the lector Majorinus, who was succeeded around 313 by Donatus of Casae Nigrae, after whom the movement was named.

The Donatists held that sacraments administered by traditores were invalid, so that those baptised by them had to be rebaptised: a continuation of Cyprian's insistence on a pure church. They appealed to Constantine, who referred the case to the council of Rome under Miltiades (313) and the council of Arles (314), which both found for Caecilian. An inquiry cleared Felix in 315, and in 316 Constantine judged in person at Milan. He then tried coercion (317-321), which produced Donatist martyrs, before tolerating them. Under Constans the mission of Paul and Macarius (347) brought violence and the exile of Donatus; Julian allowed the exiles to return in 362, and under Parmenian the Donatists became the majority church in Numidia and much of Africa.

Augustine's writings, the conference of Carthage in 411 and imperial laws of 405 and 412 finally suppressed the Donatist church, though it survived into the sixth century. W. H. C. Frend saw it as a Numidian, rural and Berber protest against Roman Carthage; later scholars (Brown, Shaw, Tilley) stress theology, martyr cult and local identity rather than nationalism. The schism was the first case of a Roman emperor intervening to decide a church dispute.
set.debate: Date of Caecilian's consecration (307 or 311/312); social versus theological explanations.

scholarship: Frend, The Donatist Church (1952)
Shaw, Sacred Violence: African Christians and Sectarian Hatred in the Age of Augustine (2011)

set.detail:
By 311 the persecution had lasted eight years and had failed to suppress Christianity. Galerius, senior Augustus, fell ill with what Lactantius describes in gruesome detail as a cancer of the genitals, an abscess that rotted and swarmed with worms, with an unbearable stench reaching the whole palace at Serdica. Lactantius and Eusebius present his illness as divine punishment. On 30 April 311 an edict issued in the names of Galerius, Licinius and Constantine (Maximinus' name is missing from Eusebius' Greek version, and he only grudgingly complied) was posted at Nicomedia.

The text, preserved in Latin by Lactantius and in Greek by Eusebius, is remarkably candid. It explains that the emperors had wanted to bring the Christians, who had abandoned the religion of their ancestors, back to a good disposition; that many had been punished, but most persisted and neither worshipped the gods nor their own God. 'Therefore, in view of our most mild clemency', the emperors permitted that 'Christians may exist again and set up the houses in which they used to meet', so long as they did nothing contrary to good order, and asked them to pray to their God for the emperors' safety and their own. A letter to the governors was to set out the details.

Galerius died a few days later, early in May 311, and was buried at Felix Romuliana. The edict was the first legal recognition of Christianity as a permitted religion (religio licita) and ended the persecution in the Balkans and the west, though Maximinus Daia, after initially complying through a circular of his prefect Sabinus, resumed persecution in his eastern territories in the autumn of 311. Compared with the 'Edict of Milan' of 313, which proclaimed religious freedom for all and ordered restitution of property, Galerius' text grants toleration grudgingly; but it was the decisive admission that the persecution had failed.

scholarship: Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (2000)
Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (1981)
